arml-2003-individual-01.title: Angles and arcs
arml-2003-individual-01.body:
Let $m\stackrel\frown{AC}=\alpha$, $m\stackrel\frown{EF}=\beta$ (an arc of the small circle) and $m\stackrel\frown{DB}=x$. The central angle $\angle EOF=\beta$, and $\triangle EOF$ is isosceles ($OE=OF$), so $\angle FEO=\dfrac{180^\circ-\beta}2$. Since $E$, $O$, $B$ are collinear, $\angle FEO=\angle DEB$, which by the intersecting-chords theorem equals $\dfrac{\alpha+x}2$. Hence $180-\beta=\alpha+x$, so $x=180-(\alpha+\beta)=180-83=97$.

**Answer: $97^\circ$**

arml-2003-individual-02.title: Combine the conditions
arml-2003-individual-02.body:
Log-right means $\log(a^2b^2)=\log c^2$, i.e. $c=ab$. A right triangle with $a\le b\le c$ has $a^2+b^2=c^2=a^2b^2$, so $b^2\left(a^2-1\right)=a^2$. This forces $a>1$ and $b^2=\dfrac{a^2}{a^2-1}$. The requirement $a\le b$ gives $\dfrac{a^2}{a^2-1}\ge a^2$, i.e. $a^2-1\le1$, so $a\le\sqrt2$. Equality occurs for $a=b=\sqrt2$, $c=2$: it is a right triangle ($2+2=4$) and $\log2+\log2=\log4$. So the largest $a$ is $\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $\sqrt2$**

arml-2003-individual-03.title: Difference of squares
arml-2003-individual-03.body:
$p-1=(4k)^2-(4m)^2=16(k-m)(k+m)$ with $k>m\ge1$. The factors $k-m$ and $k+m$ have the same parity, so $t=(k-m)(k+m)$ is odd (any odd $t\ge3$: take $k-m=1$) or a multiple of $4$ (any $t=4s\ge8$: take $k-m=2,k+m=2s$). So $p=16t+1$ with $t\in\{3,5,7,8,9,11,\dots\}$. Check: $t=3$: $49=7^2$; $t=5$: $81$; $t=7$: $113$ is prime. So the least such prime is $113=16\cdot7+1$, from $7=4^2-3^2$, i.e. $112=16^2-12^2$.

**Answer: 113**

arml-2003-individual-04.title: Digit sums
arml-2003-individual-04.body:
The digit sum of $N$ is divisible by $3$, so after removing a digit $d$ the remaining digit sum is $\equiv-d\pmod3$; the remaining number is divisible by $3$ iff $d\in\{0,3,6,9\}$. There are $300$ numbers $N$ and $3$ digits each: $900$ equally likely cases. Count the favourable ones by position.

*Units digit* $\in\{0,3,6,9\}$: choose the hundreds digit $A\in\{1..9\}$ and tens digit $B\in\{0..9\}$ with $A+B\equiv0\pmod3$ (then $C\in\{0,3,6,9\}$ is forced to be $\equiv0$): there are $3\cdot4+3\cdot3+3\cdot3=30$ such pairs and $4$ choices of $C$, so $120$. *Tens digit* in $\{0,3,6,9\}$: likewise $120$. *Hundreds digit* in $\{3,6,9\}$: choose $B,C$ with $B+C\equiv0\pmod3$ ($4\cdot4+3\cdot3+3\cdot3=34$ pairs), then $A\in\{3,6,9\}$: $102$.

Favourable: $120+120+102=342$, probability $\dfrac{342}{900}=\dfrac{19}{50}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{19}{50}=0.38$**

arml-2003-individual-05.title: Subtract collinear pairs
arml-2003-individual-05.body:
There are $5\cdot5=25$ points; removing $A$ leaves $24$, giving $\binom{24}2=276$ pairs. A pair gives a degenerate triangle iff the two points are collinear with $A$. On the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis and the line $y=x$ there are $4$ points each (besides $A$), contributing $3\binom42=18$ pairs. The other lines through $A$ containing two points of the grid are $y=2x$ (points $(1,2),(2,4)$) and $y=\frac x2$ (points $(2,1),(4,2)$): $2$ more pairs. So $n=276-18-2=256$.

**Answer: 256**

arml-2003-individual-06.title: Approximate the square root
arml-2003-individual-06.body:
$11111^2=123454321$, so $\sqrt{123456789}=\sqrt{11111^2+2468}$. By the binomial approximation, $\sqrt{11111^2+2468}\approx11111+\dfrac{2468}{2\cdot11111}-\dfrac{2468^2}{8\cdot11111^3}=11111+0.111061\ldots-5\cdot10^{-7}$, so the fractional part is $0.11106\ldots$. The nearest unit fraction is $\frac19=0.1111\ldots$ ($\frac18=0.125$ and $\frac1{10}=0.1$ are much farther). So $n=9$.

**Answer: 9**

arml-2003-individual-06.title: Series trick
arml-2003-individual-06.body:
Let $x=\sqrt{123456789}$. Then $\dfrac x{10^5}=\sqrt{0.0123456789}\approx\sqrt{\dfrac1{10^2}+\dfrac2{10^3}+\dfrac3{10^4}+\cdots}$; with $S=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac k{10^{k+1}}=\frac1{81}$ this suggests $\dfrac x{10^5}\approx\dfrac19$, i.e. $x\approx11111.\overline1$, fractional part $\approx\frac19$.

**Answer: 9**

arml-2003-individual-07.title: Factor
arml-2003-individual-07.body:
$1001001001=1001\cdot10^6+1001=1001\left(10^6+1\right)=1001\left(10^2+1\right)\left(10^4-10^2+1\right)=1001\cdot101\cdot9901=7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot101\cdot9901$, and $9901$ is prime (no prime up to $99$ divides it). A divisor that includes $9901$ and any other prime factor is at least $7\cdot9901>10^4$. A divisor without $9901$ divides $7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot101$, and its largest value below $10^4$ is $7\cdot13\cdot101=9191<9901$ (the product $11\cdot13\cdot101=14443$ is too large). So the largest factor below $10{,}000$ is $9901$.

**Answer: 9901**

arml-2003-individual-08.title: Double roots
arml-2003-individual-08.body:
Let the common tangent be $y=mx+b$. Then $g(x)=f(x)-(mx+b)$ has double roots at $x=p$ and $x=q$, so $g(x)=(x-p)^2(x-q)^2=x^4-2(p+q)x^3+\left(p^2+4pq+q^2\right)x^2-2pq(p+q)x+p^2q^2$. Compare coefficients: $x^3$: $-2(p+q)=4$, so $p+q=-2$. $x^2$: $p^2+4pq+q^2=-16$, i.e. $(p+q)^2+2pq=-16$, so $4+2pq=-16$ and $pq=-10$. (Indeed $p,q=-1\pm\sqrt{11}$ with common tangent $y=46x-105$.)

**Answer: $-10$**

arml-2003-individual-tb1.title: Power of a point
arml-2003-individual-tb1.body:
Let $E$ be the point diametrically opposite $D$, so $DE$ is the diameter and $\angle DAE=90^\circ$. In right triangle $DAE$ with altitude $AC$ ($C$ is the foot, on $DE$), $AD^2=DC\cdot DE$, so $DE=\dfrac{1600}{DC}$. We need $DE$ an integer, so $DC$ divides $1600=2^6\cdot5^2$. The condition $DC<OD=\frac{DE}2$ gives $DC<\frac{800}{DC}$, i.e. $DC^2<800$, $DC\le28$. The divisors of $1600$ up to $28$ are $1,2,4,5,8,10,16,20,25$: $9$ values.

**Answer: 9**

arml-2003-individual-tb2.title: Write $x=n+h$
arml-2003-individual-tb2.body:
Let $x=n+h$ with $n=[x]$ an integer and $0\le h<1$. Then $\dfrac{n+h}n=\dfrac{2002}{2003}$ gives $h=-\dfrac n{2003}$. Since $0\le h<1$ we need $-2002\le n\le-1$ ($n=0$ is not allowed). The least $x$ comes from $n=-2002$: $h=\dfrac{2002}{2003}$ and $x=-2002+\dfrac{2002}{2003}=\dfrac{2002(1-2003)}{2003}=-\dfrac{2002^2}{2003}=-\dfrac{4008004}{2003}$ (in lowest terms since $2003$ is prime).

**Answer: $-\dfrac{4008004}{2003}$**

arml-2003-individual-tb3.title: Sum of six consecutive integers
arml-2003-individual-tb3.body:
If the smallest is $x$, the sum is $x+(x+1)+\dots+(x+5)=6x+15=3(2x+5)$. So $41\cdot43\cdot N=3(2x+5)$, and $3\mid N$. The least possible $N$ is $3$: then $2x+5=41\cdot43=1763$ and $x=879$. Larger $N$ give larger $x$, so the least smallest integer is $879$.

**Answer: 879**
